old: A 1516 travel account carried a description of people said to lose all restraint, and English kept the word for it.
It traces back to a Malay term meaning to go on a killing spree.
Portuguese amouco passed the word along from Malay amuk before English picked it up.
clues: This adverb describes a way of behaving, and it reached English through accounts of the people of Malaysia and Java.
It means acting in a wild, frenzied, uncontrolled rush, far more violent than merely rowdy. Its Malay ancestor meant to go on a killing spree.
Almost always follows the verb run, as when toddlers run ___ at a party. An unrelated Khmer word spelled the same way means to steam in banana leaves.
